prompt: It is January 2, 2019. I would like to outperform the S&P 500 over the next five years. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy? Answer as of that date.
reply:
# 10 Stock Picks as of January 2, 2019

I actually know how 2019–2023 turned out, so I can't give you a truly blind 2019 answer. Any list I write is at least partly shaped by hindsight. So I've done two things below. First, I built a list using only reasoning that was common in January 2019, including some consensus favorites that later disappointed. Second, I show how those picks actually performed.

## The list (reasoning as of January 2, 2019)

**Background:** The S&P 500 just fell about 20% from its September 2018 peak. The Fed has been raising rates, and the US–China tariff fight is ongoing. Many high-quality companies are cheaper than they've been in years.

| # | Stock | Why buy it (Jan 2019 view) | Main risk (Jan 2019 view) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Microsoft** (MSFT) | Azure is growing about 75% a year, and Office 365 brings steady subscription revenue | Premium valuation |
| 2 | **Alphabet** (GOOGL) | Dominates search; YouTube and Cloud are underappreciated; large cash pile | Regulators, rising costs |
| 3 | **Amazon** (AMZN) | AWS earns high margins, and advertising is a new profit engine; down about 25% from its peak | Heavy spending, antitrust |
| 4 | **Facebook** (FB) | Down about 40% after Cambridge Analytica, yet still growing over 30% a year at a modest valuation | Privacy regulation, higher spending |
| 5 | **Nvidia** (NVDA) | Down about 50% from its peak because unsold crypto-mining chips are clogging the channel; data center and AI demand look like a long-term trend | Cyclical chip demand, how long the inventory glut lasts |
| 6 | **Visa** (V) | Benefits from the long-term shift from cash to cards | Regulation, fintech competitors |
| 7 | **UnitedHealth** (UNH) | Steady growth, with the Optum division growing even faster | "Medicare for All" political risk |
| 8 | **JPMorgan** (JPM) | Best-run large bank, cheap at around 11x earnings, benefits from higher rates | Recession, flattening yield curve |
| 9 | **Disney** (DIS) | The Fox deal is closing and the Disney+ streaming service launches in late 2019 | Cost of building streaming, cable TV decline |
| 10 | **Boeing** (BA) | Record deliveries, large order backlog, heavy buybacks | 737 MAX: the investigation into the Lion Air crash is still ongoing |

## How it actually played out (Jan 2, 2019 → Dec 29, 2023)

Figures are approximate, based on split-adjusted prices from memory, and exclude dividends.

| Stock | Approx. return |
|---|---|
| Nvidia | **~+1,350%** |
| Microsoft | ~+270% |
| Alphabet | ~+165% |
| Meta (Facebook) | ~+160% |
| UnitedHealth | ~+110% |
| Amazon | ~+95% |
| Visa | ~+95% |
| JPMorgan | ~+70% |
| Disney | ~−18% |
| Boeing | ~−19% |
| **S&P 500 (with dividends)** | **~+105%** |

## What this teaches

- **The equal-weighted portfolio beat the index by a wide margin**, averaging about +230%. Almost all of that edge came from one stock: Nvidia.
- **Without Nvidia, the other nine averaged about +104%,** roughly the same as the index. The median stock also did about as well as the index.
- **About half the picks trailed the S&P 500** once dividends are counted. Boeing (two 737 MAX crashes) and Disney (heavy streaming losses) actually lost money, even though both were popular, well-argued picks at the time.
- **Beating the index usually comes from a few big winners you held onto.** Nvidia fell more than 50% again in 2022, and many holders sold before it recovered.
- **Most professional fund managers fail to beat the S&P 500 over five-year periods.** An index fund, or a small "satellite" portion of stock picks alongside one, is the sensible default.

If you're asking because you want to invest now, in 2026, this historical exercise won't tell you what to buy today. I'm happy to walk through a framework for evaluating stocks instead, but for real money, consider a fee-only financial advisor.
